newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Fed set for the year of the target in 97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Fed set for the year of the target in 97.

text.p: The Federal Reserve, gearing up for a final push toward price stability, may officially adopt an inflation target in 1997 to home in on its often-proclaimed policy goal.
"Setting a target may be the best way for the public to understand policy," one Fed official told Reuters.
The Fed wants to conquer the last anti-inflation frontier after it successfully drove inflation lower in an economy growing at a pace historically associated with price pressures, the source said.

The source said most senior Fed officials privately support targeting a specific inflation level because this would enhance the Fed's credibility and make it easier for financial markets to interpret policy moves.

However, the source cautioned that Fed officials are reluctant to adopt an official target without formal hearings in Congress, which oversees the independent central bank and has assigned to it a dual anti-inflation, maximum-employment mandate.
"There are several issues still to be resolved," the source added.

Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan -- an early advocate of an inflation target -- told Reuters in a recent interview, "We're trying to create the conditions where people make their decisions about the future in the expectation the purchasing power of the currency will be about the same as it is now."
Jordan, however, admitted one problem with price stability is "how to measure it."

The notion of price stability or zero inflation has been muddled by the suspected upward bias in the main measure of U.S. inflation, the Consumer Price Index, that some experts say overstates inflation by about a percentage point.
New York Fed President William McDonough, has proposed targeting core CPI in a 0.5- to 2.0-percent range to allow for a likely margin of error in the popular gauge of inflation.
McDonough recently told a conference Fed officials looked at what may be the best "price indicator... to guide policy and came to the conclusion the core CPI is in fact the best."
Targeting a CPI range would allow for a margin of error and prevent overshooting a zero-inflation goal.
Lee Hoskins, Jordan's predecessor at the Cleveland Fed, asserted that adopting a price target will not enhance the Fed's credibility -- unless it is pegged to a timeframe.
"You can't just say 'We want price stability and that's the goal," Hoskins said. "You have to have a time commitment, like a multi-year target to achieve it."

Chief economist Lou Crandall at Wrightson and Associates, a former Fed staffer, said "inflation targets are the darling of the (anti-inflation) hawks" who favor strict timeframes and specific inflation levels rather than broader targets, such as nominal Gross Domestic Product.
"What you want to do is reach your target and then announce you have a target," said Crandall who predicted the Fed will pledge to uphold price stability once it is reached.

One drawback with inflation targets, though, is that they have been historically adopted by central banks struggling to fight a credibility or an inflation problem -- not the case of the United States in the mid-1990s. Furthermore, they do not address what policy should be during recessions.
Former Fed vice chairman Alan Blinder said the Fed needs a dual inflation and employment target in order to abide by its dual price/growth mandate.
"The Fed should have some combination target, like the core CPI and the civilian unemployment rate," Blinder said.
Blinder also stressed that short-term attempts to shore up growth in a downturn should take place only if this does not conflict with the long-term anti-inflation fight.
"Posting a price target -- and that would certainly be a price range -- would remove the mystery about what that target is and would better inform markets," Blinder added.

Privately, Fed officials admit the main drawback in the Fed's otherwise successful anti-inflation policy has been a difficulty in conveying its intention to the marketplace -- all too often resulting in wild swings in long-term interest rates the Fed does not control.
"The Fed does not have a clear, achievable mandate," said St. Louis Fed president Thomas Melzer, recently commenting on the Fed's implementing legislation.

"I am convinced that uncertainty about the Fed's monetary policy goals and methods produces greater volatility in markets than would otherwise occur," concluded Melzer, who favors revamping Fed legislation.
